messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: optimization
messages.body_plain:
Yes, I did automatic differentiation way back in 1980's, with user defined functions.

I'll bow out, but if you ever need to optimize a function without analytical derivatives, check out BOBYQA.

On Friday, November 30, 2012 9:45:25 PM UTC, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The auto-diff does analytic derivatives on the program.
>
> There's a pretty good description on the Wikipedia:
>
>
>
> http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automatic_differentiation
>
>
>
> We use reverse mode with a templated C++ implementation of
>
> what they call taping.
>
>
>
> Basically, anything where you can code the probability
>
> function in C++, we can differentiate it (as can the other
>
> auto-diff packages).  You can use loops, recursion, function
>
> calls, whatever.  You do have to either (a) use one of
>
> the functions in our library, or (b) use something that
>
> templates the variables for which you want to take the gradient.
>
>
>
> The penalty in speed is about a factor of four over just
>
> the probability function. This is independent of
>
> dimension (unlike finite diffs, which is slow in every implementation and
>
> even slower if you do something less naive than a single
>
> point).  Space usage can be bad for iterative
>
> algorithms because it stores the entire expression tree leading
>
> to the log probability in a forward pass before applying the
>
> chain rule in a backward pass.
>
>
>
> - Bob
>
>
>

>
> >>
>
> >> down (or even be able to write down) the derivativesï¿½it uses automatic
>

>
> >> differentiation to compute the derivatives of the log-joint function.

>
> >>
>
> >> differentiable but whose derivatives don't have a closed form then
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] broadcasting for binary ops
messages.body_plain:
The only major issue with adding broadcasting is that it can sometimes trip up unsuspecting users.  For instance, working with python I've occasionally had bugs that were caused by broadcasting causing expressions to work that probably should have failed due to size mismatches.  This then produced a surprising error somewhere else that was hard to track back to the origin.  A more minor issue is that it may expose Stans weaknesses with indexing, reshaping, etc as people try to do more sophisticated things.

All of that said, I too love generality and it can be an incredibly convenient feature to have for large models.  Being able to avoid multiple for loops to do simple operations is incredibly handy and the rules of it are pretty simple to understand once explained.

Cheers,
Marcus

>
> Thanks for the pointer -- I'll read up on their design.
>
>
> > It's a really nice
> > feature, but it is primarily for efficiencies which we are unlikely to realize.
>
> It's all coding convenience for us -- it won't be
> faster than a loop, unlike the broadcasting you did
> for the auto-dif lib.
>
>
> > I would say focus on broadcasting for the scalar vs vector/matrix/array case.  This is consistent with what we're
> > already doing for scalar-matrix/vector ops +, -, * and /.
>
> That's what I'm implementing first.
>
> I also thought the more general cases would be confusing
> to doc and for users.  But they're pretty easy to do, so
> they're catnip to a generality-obsessed programmer like me.
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  I'm also going to add proper conditional if-else statements
>       and probably while loops and maybe plain old for loops.

>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] optimization
messages.body_plain:
That is indeed the definitive implementation. It's really annoying
that it's in Fortran. Not just because it's a pain, but more
importantly because I don't want to make Stan users install a Fortran
compiler.

There's no question that Newton's method is completely impractical in
many situations, and that we're (I'm) going to want LBFGS. It's not
that hard to implement the unconstrained version, it's just a little
bit of a pain. Fortunately we don't have to worry about box
constraints, because we're already transforming everything to an
unconstrained space.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] duma
messages.body_plain:
On 11/30/12 5:47 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> I tried to run test-unit linking to the duma library
>
> http://duma.sourceforge.net/

Thanks for running this.  I'm a big fan of automatic
fault detection.

> which is intended "to detect buffer overruns and under-runs in C and C++ programs". It alleges there are 37 such
> problems in Stan:
>
> |
> Segmentation fault
> make: *** [runtest/test/io/reader] Error 139
> DUMA 2.5.15 (shared library, NO_LEAKDETECTION)

... BIG SNIP...

>
> There is a detailed explanation as to what to do at
>
> http://duma.sourceforge.net/README.txt

Their README says this:

-------------------
DUMA uses the virtual memory hardware of your computer to place an inaccessible
memory page immediately after (or before, at the user's option) each memory
allocation. When software reads or writes this inaccessible page, the hardware
issues a segmentation fault, stopping the program at the offending instruction.
It is then trivial to find the erroneous statement using your favorite
debugger. In a similar manner, memory that has been released by free() is made
inaccessible, and any code that touches it will get a segmentation fault.
--------------------

I don't think this strategy is sound for our arena-based
memory usage, which allocates contiguous subblocks within
a larger block of memory.  I'm less skeptical about the
locations that don't touch that memory.  I rarely use
stepwise debuggers myself because I find them incredibly hard
to follow compared to instrumenting with print statements.
But this is a good excuse to try it out and see where it
thinks the seg fault's coming from.

Partly I'm thinking that if we had segfault issues all over
like this, that they'd actually be tickled by our tests
or our regular usage, and as far as I know, we've never seen
this happen.

> It might be nice if Jenkins linked to duma by default.

I'm all for adding it to Jenkins once I'm convinced it's
not going to just give us a long list of false positives.
If it's slow, I'm sure Daniel could configure it like the
model tests to run daily rather than on every commit.

- Bob

messages.subject: pushed if-then-else and while statements
messages.body_plain:
For the next release, there is now:

   1.  Comparison operators:  <, >, <=, >=, !=, ==

   2.  Boolean operators:  !, &&, ||

   3.  If-then-else statements

   4.  While loops

All of these constructs are directly translated to their
C++ equivalents, and I preserved the C++ syntax and operator
orders and precedences for Stan.

So far, I haven't vectorized or allowed any of the operators
to broadcast, so the comparison and boolean operators only
accept primitive types (int or real).

I still need to add tests for parsing/compilation in
test/gm/parser and add more doc.  But it looks like it's
all working.

I still need a good example for while loops!  Is there some
kind of iterative algorithm that would make sense to have in
a model where the loop bounds aren't characterized by a simple
integer sequence for (i in L:U) { ... }?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I introduced the bug and I just pushed a fix to revert
it to where it was before.   I'm really glad you (Jiqiang)
caught the bug.

The problem is that I wrote a new log_prob method in
the generated model code that works on double types.
But I forgot to change the propto template param
from true to false so that the values weren't all zero.

And I just realized that if I do fix the propto template param
to be false, then the log probability value won't be the
same as that returned by the model --- it would include
the constant terms.   And I think that's too confusing.

So I just took it out pending more thought on the right
thing to to do.

- Bob

My understanding is that LBFGS (without bounds) had a relaxed license, if any,  but LBFGS-B 2.0 had much more stringent copyright license, copyright to the publishers of the original journal, so you basically had to stay with the Fortran.

R uses LBFGS-B 2.0, last time I looked.

However, there is a LBFGS-B 3.0 which had a revised algorithm, released 2011, and this has the much more relaxed 3-clause license, and no copyright to any journal.

I have converted LBFGS-B 3.0 to Java, but it was not a trivial task. Problems with GOTO's and return values of arguments. Took me a few weeks of effort. So I would expect a similar conversion to C to take a few weeks.

The code for LBFGS is considerably different (and shorter) than LBFGS-B.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Estimating step_size in diag_nuts
messages.body_plain:
Oops, I just replied to Yuanjun instead of to the list. Here's my
response, which more or less echoes Bob's:

1. There is a sort of an identifiability problem with the global step
size epsilon and the vector of per-variable step sizes—one could
multiply the global step size by x and divide all of the local step
sizes by x and get the same result. If the overall magnitude of the
step_sizes vector changed dramatically, this would throw off the
estimation of the global step size parameter. So it's more stable if
we ensure that only the relative weights in the step size vector
change, and let the overall step size be controlled by epsilon.

2. There is useful information throughout each trajectory. Any
in-slice point is (more or less) a valid sample from the posterior, so
there's no reason to throw away that information when estimating the
relative variances of each dimension. So that's why I use all of the
in-slice points on the trajectory, rather than just the point that's
ultimately sampled. This removes one source of noise when estimating
the variances.

Hope that helps!

Matt

messages.subject: Parallelization Framework
messages.body_plain:
Hey,

So I've been working on a little side project implementing parallel tempering (aka replica exchange) in Stan.  Currently I have a functional but non-parallel implementation.  It needs a little testing yet, but it's basically there.

The next step, of course, is to parallelize it.  Unlike running multiple chains, this cannot be done by running multiple independent processes because there are interactions between the running chains.  This leads me to my current question: what do we want to use to parallelize Stan.

Here are the two options as I see it:

1) Threading.  Multiple threads spawned on a single machine using shared memory/locking/etc for communication.

Pros: Convenient when you only have a single machine to run on.  A little easier to work with when parallelization is very simple (like running multiple independent chains or with only simple interactions).
Cons: Cannot distribute across multiple machines.  Getting threading right can sometimes be tricky due to non-threadsafe libraries.

2) MPI.  This is the standard API for distributing across multiple machines.  Communication is done using the MPI interfaces and is done over a network.

Pros: Easy to distribute over any number of cores/machines.  No thread safety issues, as each instance runs as a separate process.
Cons: A little harder to setup sometimes and probably harder than it needs to be for a single machine.  May not work well on Windows as it requires shared file system (I have no experience here though).  A little harder to work with when parallelization is simple but still requires communication (like with parallel tempering).

In both of these cases, there are good boost libraries available to make the code itself cross-platform.

What do people think?  Am I missing something entirely?  Neither of these consider low-level parallelization (things like CUDA, OpenMP, etc) but I think that's a separate discussion.

If left to my own devices, I would probably lean towards an MPI based implementation even though threads might be easier.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Parallelization Framework
messages.body_plain:
The decision's usually based on hardware and scalability concerns.

My understanding is that threads (a) are much faster, but (b) only
scale up to the number of cores before throughput begins to go down
rather than up.  So if we're targeting one machine, threads seem
like the right choice.  They also allow shared memory of the model
more easily if that's an issue.

I don't have experience coding either one in C++.

We'd like to have threads for other purposes, so sorting that
out in Boost would be great.  Unlike most of the other Boost
libs, their thread lib is not header only and needs to be compiled
on a per-platform basis.

The only synchronization issue I'm aware of is with auto-dif,
and there's an implementation with thread-local storage (not even
sure if that's available on all platforms yet) that's safe (but
about 15--20% slower in a single thread compared to using regular
storage.

- Bob

On 12/4/12 4:24 PM, Yuanjun Gao wrote:
> Dear Bob,
>
> I attached my code and the method I use for leapfrog and covariance matrix estimation in the E-mail. What I have done is :
> 1. Added a function "nondiag_leapfrog" in "stan/mcmc/util.hpp" to implement the leapfrog with a matrix
> 2. Added the file in stan/mcmc/nuts_nondiag.hpp to implement the sampler class for nondiag matrix
> 3. Modified "stan/gm/command.hpp" by adding an option "--nondiag_matrix" and writing the corresponding item in "--help".
> By adding this option, the sampler "nuts_nondiag" will be called.

> So to use my sampler, just do
>
> ./bernoulli --nondiag_mass --data=bernoulli.Rdata

Perfect -- that's exactly what we'd sketched out, so I'm glad
it was workable.

> Thank you for your information about trangularView. Since I am using the Cholesky decomposition of the mass matrix, I
> think it will help the program a lot. I guess it can also be used in estimating covariance by saving half of the
> computation. But since I will have exams in the following weeks, my work on that may be quite slow
>
> Right now the thing that is bothering me is that in order to implement the leapfrog method, I have to use the location
> and momentum parameters, which are of the type vectors instead of matrix. Right now I solve it by using
> "Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd>" to solve the problem. Which means that for each leapfrog, I'll have to create three
> matrix. This is basically what I didï¿½
>
>     //The nondiagonal leapfrog implemented
>      double nondiag_leapfrog(stan::model::prob_grad& model,
>                                 std::vector<int> z,
>                                 const Eigen::MatrixXd& _cov_L,
>                                 std::vector<double>& x, std::vector<double>& m,
>                                 std::vector<double>& g, double epsilon,
>                                 std::ostream* error_msgs = 0,
>                                 std::ostream* output_msgs = 0) {
>            Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd> x_mat(x.data(),x.size(),1);
>            Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd> m_mat(m.data(),m.size(),1);
>            Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd> g_mat(g.data(),g.size(),1);
>    ï¿½ï¿½ï¿½
> }
>
> I think this is where the inefficiency lies, but I am not sure how to improve it since I am not familiar with the
> interface of Eigen with other data structure in C++. Could you help me with that?

The way to answer questions about which part of the code's
inefficient, you need a profiler.  In general, the compiler is
so clever that it's pretty much impossible for humans to tell
what's going to be efficient, except at a very coarse level.
For more information on C++ optimization, you could start with this
(book length) survey:

    http://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf

The Eigen implementation uses expression templates, which can
be a bit subtle to optimize.  Here's the general story on Map:

   http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TutorialMapClass.html

You need to track memory allocation and copy operations.
When you do this:

     Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd> x_mat(x.data(),x.size(),1);

it will construct an instance of Eigen::Map.  But
it doesn't copy any data or do any allocation (except on the
function call stack -- the heap allocation with malloc or
new is what's expensive).

The map just holds a pointer to the underlying data.  Then when it's
used, it reads from the mapped data rather than its own data.  This
can have a bit of overhead from the constructor call, but it's only
a couple operations -- that is, you shouldn't notice the time it takes.

The one thing to watch out for is copies, which will happen if
you ever try to assign the map to a regular matrix or return it
in a function that returns a matrix:

    std::vector<double> v = ...;
    Map<VectorXd> v_map(&v[0],v.size());   // no alloc, no elt copy
    VectorXd v_copy = v_map;               // alloc, elt copies

Note that we can't use C++11 features due to restrictions from R
and CRAN (they're way way behind the times), so you can't use the
std::vector .data() method.  Instead, you need to do this:

     Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd> x_mat(&x[0],x.size(),1);

the &x[0] will create a reference to the start of the matrix (same
behavior, uglier syntax).

For efficiency, Eigen specializes the template for matrices to
templates for vectors and row vectors:

matrix:         Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic>  == MatrixXd
column vector:  Matrix<double,Dynamic,1>        == VectorXd
row vector:     Matrix<double,1,Dynamic>        == RowVectorXd

So you probably want to map vectors (or row vectors depending
on usage) rather than matrices, as in this:

   Map<VectorXd> x_mat(&x[0],x.size());

or RowVectorXd, depending on how it will be used
The reference to x[0], "&x[0]", will do the same thing
as .data() in a much uglier way -- return the pointer to the
initial point in the data array.

The other thing we could do is just replace the std::vector with
an Eigen vector.  That'd probably be more efficient in that it
doesn't even need the lightweight view wrapper.  The only reason it's
std::vector now is that we wrote the first version before
the matrix lib!

- Bob

> On Dec 4, 2012, at 3:29 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
>
>> http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/QuickRefPage.html#QuickRef_DiagTriSymm
>>
>> If M is a lower triangular matrix, replace the use of
>> M in arithmetic/solver operations with:
>>
>>  M.triangularView<Eigen::Lower>()
>>
>> In cases where the type of M is templated (you probably won't
>> need this), you'd write:
>>
>>  M.template triangularView<Eigen::Lower>()
>>
>> If M is symmetric, replace uses of it with:
>>
>>  M.selfAdjointView<Eigen::Lower>()
>>
>> This treats the upper triangle as matching the lower triangle
>> and speeds up operations in the same way that triangular does.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>>
>>

messages.subject: comparison and boolean operators, conditional and while statements
messages.subject_clean: comparison and boolean operators, conditional and while statements
messages.body_plain:
I just pushed a finished version of boolean
operators (binary &&, ||, unary !), comparison
operators (<, <=, >, >=, ==, !=), conditional
statements (if, else if, else), and loop statements
(while).  They all have the same syntax (including
precedence and associativity) and semantics as in C++.

So far, nothing is vectorized, so the boolean operators and
conditionals only apply to primitive int or real types.
As in C++ (and in R, I just checked), non-zero values
are "true" and zero values "false".  So the conditionals
and while loops

I wrote general template metaprograms to vectorize
unary and binary ops.  There's really no efficiency gain
here over just writing the loops in Stan, so I haven't
put it in yet.  After more thought, I've come to agree
with Marcus that it's least confusing if we just allow
either exactly matching type or scalar arguments.  That is,
no broadcasting 1D arrays to 2D arrays or vectors to matrices.
If we want that, we can go with an explicit syntax like Eigen's.

- Bob

messages.subject: clang 3.2
messages.body_plain:
clang 3.2 is scheduled to be released December 16. So, if there are problems with it, we need to catch them quickly. Otherwise, they are more likely to delay the fix until 3.2.1 is released.

There are some binary RC2s here

http://llvm.org/pre-releases/3.2/rc2/

including an experimental one for Windows (actually, they have had experimental binaries for Windows since 3.1). If that works it would be great because there are probably some people that don't have enough RAM to compile some models on Windows.

For me, test-unit passes if all of the following are commented out:

>From make/os_linux
ifeq (clang++,$(CC_TYPE))
#  CFLAGS += -std=c++0x
#  CFLAGS_GTEST += -DGTEST_USE_OWN_TR1_TUPLE
#  CFLAGS += -stdlib=libc++

>From src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp
//  EXPECT_TRUE(is_parsable("src/test/gm/model_specs/function_signatures7.stan"));

If you uncomment  CFLAGS += -std=c++0x and CFLAGS_GTEST += -DGTEST_USE_OWN_TR1_TUPLE and use a version of boost  <= 1.51, then there are parser errors with O > 0. On one hand, sensitivity to the optimization level is a bit suspicious. On the other hand, you get the same behavior from clang 3.1.

Ben

messages.subject: Explicit integration with RMHMC
messages.body_plain:
I thought some people here might be interested in this:

http://arxiv.org/abs/1211.3759

Girolami and others have come up with a way to perform Riemann Manifold HMC with an explicit integration method, making it much more efficient.  I haven't gone through it in detail yet, but it looks very promising and the trick they use to do it is very simple but fairly clever, ie, changing from Hamiltonian dynamics to Lagrangian dynamics.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
The builds being broken on Jenkins is blocking the
release of a new version of Stan.  Not to mention
totally stressing me out because I have no idea how to
even begin to debug the problem.

Were the problems introduced by a new dependency
on C++11?   I remember deciding that we would have no
dependencies on C++11 features in Stan itself, but that
someone wanted to add some C++11 features to the tests,
which at the time, seemed OK.  If that's what's breaking
our builds, I think we should reverse that decision and
not depend on C++11 in the tests, either.

It seems like like compiler support and API support (Eigen and Boost)
is even flakier than for pre-C++11.  We're probably also doing
things wrong because I don't know what has changed from version
to version.  All the issues I see are buried in libs where we
don't seem to have any control (I include a new offering below).

I can't even get compiled with clang++ -O0 with Ben's suggestions,
putting the following in stan/make

    CFLAGS += -std=c++0x

and removing from stan/make/os_mac

    CFLAGS_GTEST += -Wno-c++11-extensions

The compiler exits in the middle of an Eigen library:

-------------------------------
clang++ -I src -I lib/eigen_3.1.2 -I lib/boost_1.52.0 -O3 -Wall -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1 -DBOOST_NO_DECLTYPE -std=c++0x
-Wno-unused-function -Wno-tautological-compare   -c -o bin/stan/math/matrix.o src/stan/math/matrix.cpp
In file included from src/stan/math/matrix.cpp:4:
In file included from src/stan/math/matrix.hpp:12:
In file included from lib/eigen_3.1.2/Eigen/Dense:1:
In file included from lib/eigen_3.1.2/Eigen/Core:248:
lib/eigen_3.1.2/Eigen/src/Core/util/Memory.h:713:23: error: no member named 'forward' in namespace
       'std'
       ::new(p) T(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
                  ~~~~~^
lib/eigen_3.1.2/Eigen/src/Core/util/Memory.h:713:31: error: 'Args' does not refer to a value
       ::new(p) T(std::forward<Args>(args)...);
                               ^
lib/eigen_3.1.2/Eigen/src/Core/util/Memory.h:710:26: note: declared here
     template<typename... Args>
                          ^
2 errors generated.
make: *** [bin/stan/math/matrix.o] Error 1

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Explicit integration with RMHMC
messages.body_plain:
Marcus

Yup, I brought that to the attention of the local Stan group as soon as it came out.  Unfortunately there are some subtleties to their method - they not only transform to a Lagrangian perspective but also make some approximations to the resulting integrator.  This kills the symplectness (and hence long term stability) of the integrator -and- degrades the error from eps^2 to eps.  They even admit that the new integrator is only advantageous in low dimensions (see their experiments section) where RMHMC wouldn't be necessary anyways.  But the integrator is a serious issue in RMHMC and we're definitely paying attention!

-Mike

I haven't gone through it in detail yet, but it looks very promising and the trick they use to do it is very simple but fairly clever, ie, changing from Hamiltonian dynamics to Lagrangian dynamics.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus

On Friday, December 7, 2012 6:31:34 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The builds being broken on Jenkins is blocking the
> release of a new version of Stan.  Not to mention
> totally stressing me out because I have no idea how to
> even begin to debug the problem.
>
> Were the problems introduced by a new dependency
> on C++11?   I remember deciding that we would have no
> dependencies on C++11 features in Stan itself, but that
> someone wanted to add some C++11 features to the tests,
> which at the time, seemed OK.  If that's what's breaking
> our builds, I think we should reverse that decision and
> not depend on C++11 in the tests, either.

I think there are two separate issues here: One is whether the tests should utilize features that are unique to the C++11 standard, which I guess Daniel has good reason to want. The other is whether Stan itself should adhere to the C++11 standard even if we are not using any of its unique features like decltype or lambda functions or whatever.

I think the problems we are having are related to the second issue, but it is a good goal to target the standard. If -std is unspecified, it defaults to g++99, which is not an actual standard. The reason why I think we are utilizing some quirky undefined behavior is that we are having more success with the old compilers. As far as I know, all versions of (pure) g++ up to 4.6.x are passing test-unit. It is g++-4.7 and clang-3.1 and the forthcoming release of each that are having trouble, plus mingw on Windows. That mingw is close to g++-4.6, but I can successfully cross-compile to Windows, so I think we would be okay if Jenkins weren't mysteriously dying.

> I can't even get compiled with clang++ -O0 with Ben's suggestions,
> putting the following in stan/make
>
>     CFLAGS += -std=c++0x
>
> and removing from stan/make/os_mac
>
>     CFLAGS_GTEST += -Wno-c++11-extensions
>
> The compiler exits in the middle of an Eigen library:

Can you get through the Eigen test suite with those options?

We should have released v1.0.4 as soon as the thing with the line numbers in the error message was fixed. And we shouldn't have tried to transition to the c++11 standard in a branch rather than in master. But I think we should keep trying to move forward rather than trying to go backward.

Ben

>
>     The builds being broken on Jenkins is blocking the
>     release of a new version of Stan.  Not to mention
>     totally stressing me out because I have no idea how to
>     even begin to debug the problem.
>
>     Were the problems introduced by a new dependency
>     on C++11?   I remember deciding that we would have no
>     dependencies on C++11 features in Stan itself, but that
>     someone wanted to add some C++11 features to the tests,
>     which at the time, seemed OK.  If that's what's breaking
>     our builds, I think we should reverse that decision and
>     not depend on C++11 in the tests, either.
>
>
> I think there are two separate issues here: One is whether the tests should utilize features that are unique to the
> C++11 standard, which I guess Daniel has good reason to want. The other is whether Stan itself should adhere to the
> C++11 standard even if we are not using any of its unique features like decltype or lambda functions or whatever.

Absolutely.  And I think it's important that we be standards compliant.

What makes this so absurdly hard with C++ is that the standard isn't
strict enough to fully determine behavior of a "compliant" compiler.
And at different optimization levels, the same compiler can make
different decisions in places where the spec's incomplete.

> I think the problems we are having are related to the second issue,

That, or incomplete implementations to the standard by either
Eigen, Boost, or the new compilers!

I don't have any strategies for working through this other than
one compiler warning and error message at a time.  But when we're
out on the cutting edge with new compilers, we can't even rely
on old newsgroup posts that work through the same problems.

> but it is a good goal to target the standard. If
> -std is unspecified, it defaults to g++99, which is not an actual standard. The reason why I think we are utilizing some
> quirky undefined behavior is that we are having more success with the old compilers. As far as I know, all versions of
> (pure) g++ up to 4.6.x are passing test-unit. It is g++-4.7 and clang-3.1 and the forthcoming release of each that are
> having trouble, plus mingw on Windows. That mingw is close to g++-4.6, but I can successfully cross-compile to Windows,
> so I think we would be okay if Jenkins weren't mysteriously dying.
>
>     I can't even get compiled with clang++ -O0 with Ben's suggestions,
>     putting the following in stan/make
>
>          CFLAGS += -std=c++0x
>
>     and removing from stan/make/os_mac
>
>          CFLAGS_GTEST += -Wno-c++11-extensions
>
>     The compiler exits in the middle of an Eigen library:
>
>
> Can you get through the Eigen test suite with those options?
>
> We should have released v1.0.4 as soon as the thing with the line numbers in the error message was fixed.

Agreed.  And part of what's making me feel so anxious about
all of this is that I introduced the error in 1.0.3 that
I so desperately want to get fixed with a release.

> And we
> shouldn't have tried to transition to the c++11 standard in a branch rather than in master. But I think we should keep
> trying to move forward rather than trying to go backward.

I think this is a timing issue.  Unless we can fix the problems
we're having now, I think we should go back as far as we have to
for a stable release.  Not having the line numbers in error messages
is a very big deal for our users and is really going to turn people
off from using Stan.

- Bob

It is hard to say that going backwards is the right direction without knowing what the problem is. That said, if we do

CFLAGS_GTEST += -std=c++0x

rather than

CFLAGS += -std=c++0x

(which I think was Daniel's original intention), then we still have test failures in src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp (for recent compilers only). However, these test failures are not that bad: stanc is parsing the .stan files fine, but parser_test.cpp does not utilize stanc. In other words, something in these headers

#include "stan/gm/ast_def.cpp"
#include "stan/gm/parser.hpp"
#include <stan/gm/generator.hpp>
#include <stan/gm/grammars/program_grammar_def.hpp>
#include <stan/gm/grammars/whitespace_grammar_def.hpp>
#include <stan/gm/grammars/expression_grammar_def.hpp>
#include <stan/gm/grammars/statement_grammar_def.hpp>
#include <stan/gm/grammars/var_decls_grammar_def.hpp>

is likely to be not compliant with the c++11 standard (i.e. we are getting the same error from both g++ >= 4.7 and clang++ >= 3.1 and with either boost 1.52 or 1.50). But no one actually parses without stanc, and it's a non-issue with the default versions of g++ on Mac and Windows anyway. So, I don't think it would be the worst thing in the world to blacklist that test, release v1.0.4, and then try to make all of Stan standard compliant for v1.0.5.

Ben

            and also work without C++11 (including testing w/o C++11).

                OR

            Require C++11 and use C++11 features.

                OR

   is Stan passing tests on all the platforms it passed tests

   Question 2:  How much work do we need to do to back out any
   C++11 dependencies in the new test code?

   Question 3:  Is there some reason (perhaps having to do with
   R, availability on the Mac or Windows, etc) that we can't move
   to always building everything with C++11 flags?

   Question 4:  What versions of clang++ and g++ under what
   backend configs do we need to support?

At the moment, there are default template parameters (and maybe some other C++11 features, not sure) in some of the tests. If we didn't specify -std=c++0x AND reverted the commits that used C++11 features, I speculate that all the tests would pass. But I think that would be overkill. AFAIK, the only test that is not passing (in some setups) is src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp, which doesn't use any C++11 specific features (that I can see) but doesn't play nice with the intersection of boost and "recent" compilers when -std=c++0x is added to CFLAGS_GTEST (or CFLAGS for that matter).

But that test is somewhat of a luxury because stanc parses everything as long as CFLAGS does not add -std=c++0x. That is why I was proposing restricting the -std=c++0x stuff to CFLAGS_GTEST, blacklisting src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp, doing v1.0.4, and then coming back to it.

>    Question 2:  How much work do we need to do to back out any
>    C++11 dependencies in the new test code?

Not that much, but I don't think it is necessary to back them out. Even if you wanted to do a release with src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp passing, you could just branch from something before 4377102d597c9bd5f011136ea21e6e995c84ac4d. The problem is that you would loose a lot of good commits since then.

>    Question 3:  Is there some reason (perhaps having to do with
>    R, availability on the Mac or Windows, etc) that we can't move
>    to always building everything with C++11 flags?

CRAN has discouraging things to say about it

http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-exts.html#Submitting-a-package-to-CRAN

but I am not sure it is prohibited on CRAN. I think g++-4.6 (and the corresponding mingw) just ignores the -std=c++0x thing, but it does implement some features that were later ratified into the C++11 standard. You can see a comparison of compilers here

https://wiki.apache.org/stdcxx/C%2B%2B0xCompilerSupport

My understanding is that the squeekiest wheel is the g++ that comes with Xcode, but I don't really know what to expect from that. We know that the standard C++ library that comes with g++-4.2.x is too old to support any C++11 features (leading to the problem with std::forward that you ran into Friday) but if you use LLVM's C++ library, clang works. So, I don't know what happens if you use the Mac hybrid of LLVM for the first pass and g++-4.2 to finish it with LLVM's C++ library.

But the main thing at the moment is that if you use --std=c++0x to build stanc, then no .stan file parses correctly, but that is independent of R and CRAN.

>    Question 4:  What versions of clang++ and g++ under what
>    backend configs do we need to support?

I'd say the only things we have to support are the compilers on the CRAN servers

http://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_flavors.html#r-devel-linux-x86_64-debian

even if RStan never goes onto CRAN. If RStan were to go onto CRAN in some form, then I believe you are only allowed to fail one compiler. Of those, Solaris Studio is already out because it doesn't do boost, eigen, or C++11. GCC 4.6.3 has always been passing on Linux and seems to be passing on Jenkins ATM. GCC 4.7.2 only fails the blacklistable src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp under -std=c++0x.

Clang isn't strictly necessary. But recent versions are the best compilers for Stan, so I think we should be encouraging people to use clang++ rather than contemplating regressions here. Clang isn't systematically slower in runtime, is much better in terms of RAM consumption, compile time, and availability of extra tools, and is a bit better in terms of error messages and completeness of C++11 implementation. Up until today, clang++-3.1 and clang-3.2++ RC had the same test failure as 4.7.2; now they have linker errors rather than test failures with blacklistable src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp.

> I just realized it's risky to try to test under C++11 and
> run under no C++11.  I'd rather test the same thing we run.

Agreed it would be ideal if it were possible to get everything working with CFLAGS += -std=c++0x, but also working with merely CFLAGS_GTEST += -std=c++0x. For a release and / or CRAN, we could turn off CFLAGS += -std=c++0x and turn on CFLAGS_GTEST += -std=c++0x if necessary.

> For the record, as of right now, I can run:
>
>    Platform:
>       Mac OS X 10.8.2
>    Compiler:
>       Apple clang version 4.1 (tags/Apple/clang-421.11.66) (based on LLVM 3.1svn)
>    Linker:
>       Not even sure what the default is here now that I know
>       there are so many ways it can be configured front and back and lib
>    CFLAGS:
>       ?? (I'm running the defaults, but looking at output of "make test-unit", they seem to vary)
>       -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1 -DBOOST_NO_DECLTYPE -Wno-unused-function -Wno-tautological-compare
>       ?? in building gtest, I also see -std=c++0x and then:
>             c1plus: error: unrecognized command line option "-std=c++0x"
>    CFLAGS_GTEST:
>       ?? (same issue as above -- not sure where the GTEST ones apply)

Look in make/tests, but basically if in make/os_* it says CFLAGS_GTEST += -std=c++0x but not CFLAGS += -std=c++0x, then libstan, stanc, libstanc, etc. implicitly reference -std=g++98 while the tests built by test-unit and test-models explicitly reference -std=c++0x. That would be a decent state of affairs, except that the blacklistable src/test/gm/parser_test.cpp fails for g++-4.7.x and my versions of clang++-3.1 and clang++-3.2.

> I haven't figured out a magic set of C++11 flags to let me
> compile with g++ on the same platform.

My guess is that many of the tests in test-unit will currently fail with g++-4.2.x if it uses the associated standard C++ library due to complete lack of any C++11 stuff. The thing to try is CFLAGS_GTEST += -stdlib=libc++ (and maybe CFLAGS += -stdlib=libc++), which uses LLVM's standard C++ library (and hopefully is included in Xcode; if not you can download it from llvm.org <http://llvm.org>).

Ben

I'm going to order some Stan t-shirts and need
to know what size everyone wants!  And get feedback
on design.

I was thinking of something relatively simple
like the attached shots.  I'm flexible on color,
size of logo, type of font, placement, etc.  The
layout program on:

   http://customink.com

is very flexible and the .pdf logo allows resizing
without aliasing.  The one shown is a Hanes "Beefy
T" (they're heavyweight t-shirts), but they have a range
of options.  The log is from the distro:

     stan/logos/stanlogo-main.pdf

and the URL text is Arial.  We could include more text,
but somehow "a C++ probability and sampling library"
seems too geeky.

I'm torn because I like darker t-shirts, but then I
prefer the logo non-reversed in terms of color.  And I love
ringer Ts, but they only have Gildan, and then not in the
colors I really like.

They'll be around $11 each including
shipping if we order 20 of them and $9 each if we order 50.

For an extra $7/item, we can get our names and a number
on the back sports-jersey style (sorry Matt -- couldn't
resist).

- Bob

Daniel and I put our heads together and we'll
remove the C++11 features (function template parameter
defaults) and replace them with plain old C++
(which means pushing the functions into static class
functions and putting the defaults on the class).

With that, I think we should be OK to do the
1.0.4 release without C++11 support.

In the meantime, I'll try to track down errors
we're having with C++11 compatibility.  It looks
like Ben's bringing all sorts of interesting tools
to the debugging table.

messages.subject: sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif
messages.subject_clean: sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif
messages.body_plain:
To lead with the punchline, we can pretty easily and
efficiently implement arbitrary Hessian-vector (or
row vector-Hessian) products in a single pass of efficient
forward auto-dif followed by reverse mode auto-dif of
the result.

Michael and I spent part of his first day talking
about how we could do Hessian-vector products with auto-diff.
He gave me enough hints on the so-called R operator that I could
work out the algebra and auto-dif implementation from scratch.

This will be useful for RM-HMC and for optimizations
using curvature info.

On 12/12/12 4:09 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

 > Efficient Hessian-Vector Products:
 >
 > Bishop 5.4.6
 > http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.29.6143
 > http://justindomke.wordpress.com/2009/01/17/hessian-vector-products/

What helped me the most was the doc for Theano:

   http://deeplearning.net/software/theano/tutorial/gradients.html

which presented it in a more computer-sciency way than most of
the other applied math and physics thing I looked at (like Bishop).

I then worked through the algebra and derived the R operator myself,
which is pretty trivial.  As an upside, I can now follow the discussion
in Bishop, which I never understood before.

The key is noticing that if H is the Hessian of y w.r.t. x and v
is any old vector, then the first step is noting that:

    H * v = grad_x ((grad_x y)' * v)

Then we use a little of the old lambda abstraction to create an
operator:

   R = lambda y. [ v' * (grad_x y) ]

so that

   R(y) =  v' * grad_x y

        =  v1 * dy/dx1 + v2 * dy/dx2 + ... + vK * dy/dxK

and

   H * v = grad_x R(y)

The key to making it efficient in auto-dif is to compute R(y) using
a forward-mode auto dif, then do the outer grad_x using reverse mode
on the result.  And the beauty is we only need to implement standard
templated forward-mode auto-dif once in a simple templated way and
we can then use it to do these calculations with the right initializations ---
the adjoint of x_k is initialized to v_k and Bob's your uncle.

The whole calc will probably take on the order of 2 or 3 times the
time for the basic gradient, so about 10 times the cost of the function
eval itself.

I've already implemented most of the basic forward dif, though I pulled
it out of version control ages ago because we weren't using it for anything.

After the next release, I'll pull it back into the main branch and then we
only have to implement gradients for special functions (which is much much
eaiser to do efficiently than reverse mode).

- Bob

I've not set Jenkins up before, but if someone gave me a few pointers and maybe send along the Stan-specific configuration being used I'm sure if wouldn't be too hard.  Just a thought.

As to the various standards/libs/etc I would suggest we pick a small number of reasonable platform targets with the goal being to build using only the easily available compilers/libs on those platforms.  For instance, on Linux, I would suggest we target GCC and LLVM on the latest version of a RHEL-like distribution and the latest version of Ubuntu.  Together they cover most Linux systems likely to be seen in practice.  Trying to support all possible combinations leads to madness and as enticing as new compiler features are, if no one can use them because most users platforms don't support them, then maybe it's just not worth it for now.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: platform support decisions
messages.body_plain:
Here's the story about C++ standards:

    C++98:  1998 ISO C++ Standard
    C++03:  2003 ISO C++ Technical Corrigendum
    C++11:  2011 ISO C++ Standard

I think C++98 is out of date in the sense that C++03 is
the default mode in both g++ and clang++.

I think C++11 is premature in that gtest doesn't support
it yet, nor do Eigen or Boost reliably.

So with the wisdom of Solomon and Goldilocks, I think
we should target C++03 and only C++03 for now.

For the Mac, I think we can safely restrict ourselves to the
latest Xcode versions of g++ and clang++ with their own default
libs:

    Xcode 4.5.2 g++ 4.2.1, {O=0, O=3}, C++03
    Xcode 4.5.2 clang++ 3.1, {O=0, O=3}, C++03

All four of these tests with the current repository version.

I added a new section at the top of the TestUnitStats listing
"supported" platforms.  The idea of "support" is that we won't
release unless all tests pass on these platforms.

I added this as the list of "supported" platforms on the Wiki for
the Mac.

Could someone do the same for Windows and Linux and make sure
the current tests pass?

If we can do this, I think we should roll out Stan 1.0.4 this weekend
or early next week.

- Bob

I disagree with that. I would always want to *know* if it doesn't work for some configuration; whether we want to fix it is a separate issue. If the failure is documented on the wiki, then other people will know not to waste their time on that configuration. But the only one inundating the list with configuration problems is me. I don't think we've had any user reports of configuration problems that weren't their own fault.

Also, if it "works" on one configuration but not on another, it is sometimes a bug in the code somewhere that just happens to get smoothed over  by the working configuration. Like with parser_test.cpp #including the definitions instead of the headers, our test file was essentially wrong but (mingw)g++ with enough optimization managed to get rid of the redundancies whereas other configurations didn't. We wouldn't have gotten that fixed if we had restricted ourselves to a sufficiently small number of supported configurations. We even incorrectly believed that we needed to compile stanc with optimization because we incorrectly thought the "File too big" thing was a mingw bug.

> We could open it up the public to edit and then it won't fall to
> us.

Yes, I think we should make that wiki page editable by anyone who subscribes to stan-users if that is possible. If you make it world-editable, we will have problems with spammers.

> On the Mac, g++ defaults to g++03.
>

I doubt it. Maybe it is a difference between pure g++ and Apple's llvm-g++? Do you have a link to the llvm-g++ defaults on a Mac?

> I say we wait on C++11 until it's the R default.
> That should put an end to our C++11 woes indefinitely
> unless Eigen or Boost make it their default first.

What does it mean for Eigen or Boost to make C++11 their default? AFAIK, both currently work with some subset of the C++11 features if the user specifies -std=c++0x in the makefile but continue to work with -std=c++03. I doubt either will introduce anything that only works if -std=c++0x for a long, long time. Same with R.

That said, I'm not sure we really need to be using any C++11 features in the tests, much less libstan or libstanc. But I'm not even sure what woes were actually attributable to using -std=c++0x. The parser_test.cpp problems weren't C++11 problems. There is a problem with either {g++ >= 4.7 and CFLAGS += -std=c++0x} or {clang >= 3.1 and CFLAGS += -stdlib=libc++ -std=c++98/03 -DGTEST_USE_OWN_TR1_TUPLE} but I would guess that is either attributable to Boost or Stan. There presumably is a problem with using any C++11 features with GCC's ancient C++ library that comes with Xcode, but LLVM claims that -stdlib=libc++ is known to work (I'm not sure how exactly) with g++ 4.2.

Ben

messages.subject: minimum platform support (Linux = ???)
messages.body_plain:
I want to pull back to minimum platform support in
our testing.  This will potentially make users adopt
our versions of compilers, but it makes our lives
much much easier.

The constraints from R come from its default Makeconf

   R:
     g++ -O2  (default)
     g++ -O3  (our reco upgrade)

and lead to the constraints:

   Mac:
     g++ latest XCode with -O0, -O2, -O3, default flags
     ==> 4.2.1

   Windows
      g++ latest RTools with default flags and -O2 and -03
      ==> 4.6.3

   Linux
      g++ latest stable version, with default flags and -O0, -O2, -O3
      ==> ???

I would like to support clang++, because it's what we're also using:

   Mac
     clang++ latest Xcode with -O0, -O2, -O3, default flags
     ==> 3.1

   Linux
     clang++ latest stable version, with default flags and -O0, -O2, -O3
     ==> ???

If we support the above, I feel OK leaving everything else to
our users to test.

Ben -- what's the "canonical" Linux version of g++ and clang++?
And do our tests pass on them?

Our tests all pass on Mac and Windows with the above configs.

- Bob

There isn't a "canonical" Linux anything. The most widely used personal variants are in the Ubuntu family but the toolchain varies depending on what version you are using. The most widely used server variants are in the Red Hat family, where again the toolchain varies but tends to be older than what an individual would have.

With the current Stan makefile, CC=g++ by default. On a Linux system, g++ is usually a symlink to some versioned g++ like g++-4.6. We have no way of knowing what g++ points to. I would say the expectation of the community is that any program should work with the latest stable upstream version of a compiler, which is g++-4.7.x currently (4.8 is a few months off). But the expectation of the community is that any program should typically work with some older versions of the compiler, unless there is a compelling reason why that is impossible, because Linux distributions (particularly for servers) default to compilers that were released a few years ago. For example, our own Hotfoot scientific computing servers (RHEL) have this software

https://wikis.cuit.columbia.edu/confluence/display/rcs/Hotfoot+Software

e.g. gcc-4.1 is the default but gcc-4.4 is available. That is a bit extreme but not atypical for a server.

Ben

1) Tested to work, we run test-unit and don't release if it breaks.  This is a small number of specific configurations based on what gives us good coverage and what we can manage.

Or any platform with versions of gcc >= 4.4 or clang++ >= 3.0.  This is the largest pool of configurations and ideally developers occasionally touch some on them occasionally.

Some projects handle this by leading with 2) and then following with 1).  For instance,

"Stan should work on any platform and compiler which is supported by both Eigen and Boost and has been known to work on the following system configurations <list from 2>.  Failure to work on these, or any other Eigen and Boost supported platform should be reported as a bug.  Stan is routinely tested and should always work under the following configurations: <list from 1>"

On Friday, December 14, 2012 6:33:59 PM UTC-5, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> Agreed.  Basically two tiers of supported platforms:

Yes. When I created the wiki page, I wasn't intending it to define the tiers of support, which I think is more appropriate for the manual or for mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>. I just called it "Results of test-unit for various configurations" so that we could list as many working or not working configurations that have been tested at a particular SHA. Also to have a central place where the current error messages were listed so we wouldn't have to dig through the list.

But the wiki page is something completely different now, doesn't convey Marcus' principles, doesn't make that much sense. If we say, "here are the configurations that we wouldn't release Stan without passing test-unit", then do we really need to say "and here are the SHAs where they, in fact, passed"? Users can assume test-unit passage for those configurations at any v1.0.x tag, and users shouldn't really care if those configurations happen to be temporarily broken at any intermediate commit.

The other thing that bothers me is that if we generally expect Stan to work in situations where Boost and Eigen generally work, and we find a configuration where that is not the case, we should presume it is a Stan bug, instead of saying we don't care unless it is a Tier I supported configuration. If we can conclusively say it is an Eigen bug, a Boost bug, a compiler bug, etc. and report it upstream and they acknowledge it, that is fine and we can document that Stan will not work in that situation for reasons that are out of our control. But for something like the current situation with clang-3.2 yielding weird Boost warnings and parser failures, we do not yet know where the bug is yet. That isn't necessarily a reason to hold up v1.0.4, but we should be actively trying to work on it because it could imply that the Stan code is silently doing the wrong or suboptimal thing in "working" configurations.

For stanc in particular, our tests don't really tell us whether we are generating the expected C++ code or whether it is compiling in the expected way. We just know if a .stan file parses or not. The test-models target helps a little bit here, but it is sort of blunt and we aren't paying too much attention when some model is reported to fail.

Ben

On Saturday, December 15, 2012 4:40:02 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > If we can conclusively say it is an Eigen bug, a
> > Boost bug, a compiler bug, etc. and report it upstream and they acknowledge it, that is fine and we can document that
> > Stan will not work in that situation for reasons that are out of our control.
>
> Not quite out of our control -- we can contribute patches to
> Eigen and Boost.
>
> > But for something like the current
> > situation with clang-3.2 yielding weird Boost warnings and parser failures, we do not yet know where the bug is yet.
>
> Right -- it could be in our code, the Boost libs,
> or the clang-3.2 compiler compatibility.
>
> I think the next step to debug this would be to try
> to isolate a smaller grammar for which we can produce
> the same problem.  This is a huge pain in the ass with
> the way Spirit is written, but I'll give it a go as soon
> as I can figure out how to install a clang-3.2 compiler
> that exhibits the issues you're having.
>
> The issues seem to be around their iterator pattern, which
> I literally just cut and pasted from the Boost example code.

Okay, I'm becoming increasingly convinced that it is a limitation of Boost or a lack of completeness in the example they gave. We might be in position to raise on the Spirit list now. Our parser is based on

http://boost-spirit.com/dl_more/parsing_tracking_position/stream_iterator_errorposition_parsing.cpp

which I made one small formatting change to circumvent some compiler issue with std::setw

    for(int i = 2; i < pos.column; i++) msg << ' ';
    msg << " ^-- here" << std::endl << std::endl;
//      std::setw(pos.column) << " " << "^- here";

and to make it match of our parser (although that shouldn't make any difference below).

Then I compiled it a bunch of different ways, extracted the strings from the binary, and grepped for this MultiPass thingie:

g++-4.6 -O0 stream_iterator_errorposition_parsing.cpp
strings a.out | grep MultiPass::reference > string_g++-4.6.txt
g++-4.7 -O0 stream_iterator_errorposition_parsing.cpp -std=c++0x
strings a.out | grep MultiPass::reference > string_g++-4.7.txt
g++-4.8 -O0 stream_iterator_errorposition_parsing.cpp -std=c++0x
strings a.out | grep MultiPass::reference > string_g++-4.8.txt
clang++ -O0 stream_iterator_errorposition_parsing.cpp -std=c++0x
strings a.out | grep MultiPass::reference > string_clang++1.txt
clang++ -O0 stream_iterator_errorposition_parsing.cpp -std=c++0x -stdlib=libc++
strings a.out | grep MultiPass::reference > string_clang++2.txt

(that is clang++ 3.2 BTW) And the compilers are doing very different things with it:

cat string_g++-4.6.txt # ends with char&]
static typename MultiPass::reference boost::spirit::iterator_policies::split_std_deque::unique<Value>::dereference(const MultiPass&) [with MultiPass = boost::spirit::multi_pass<std::istreambuf_iterator<char, std::char_traits<char> > >, Value = char, typename MultiPass::reference = char&]

cat string_g++-4.7.txt # ends with char]
static typename MultiPass::reference boost::spirit::iterator_policies::split_std_deque::unique<Value>::dereference(const MultiPass&) [with MultiPass = boost::spirit::multi_pass<std::istreambuf_iterator<char, std::char_traits<char> > >; Value = char; typename MultiPass::reference = char]

cat string_g++-4.8.txt # ends with char] like g++-4.7
static typename MultiPass::reference boost::spirit::iterator_policies::split_std_deque::unique<Value>::dereference(const MultiPass&) [with MultiPass = boost::spirit::multi_pass<std::istreambuf_iterator<char, std::char_traits<char> > >; Value = char; typename MultiPass::reference = char]

cat string_clang++1.txt # totally different policies than g++*
static typename MultiPass::reference boost::spirit::iterator_policies::split_std_deque::unique<char>::dereference(const MultiPass &) [Value = char, MultiPass = boost::spirit::multi_pass<std::istreambuf_iterator<char, std::char_traits<char> >, boost::spirit::iterator_policies::default_policy<boost::spirit::iterator_policies::ref_counted, boost::spirit::iterator_policies::no_check, boost::spirit::iterator_policies::buffering_input_iterator, boost::spirit::iterator_policies::split_std_deque> >]

cat string_clang++2.txt # just mangles the std::__ differently when using LLVM's C++ standard library
static typename MultiPass::reference boost::spirit::iterator_policies::split_std_deque::unique<char>::dereference(const MultiPass &) [Value = char, MultiPass = boost::spirit::multi_pass<std::__1::istreambuf_iterator<char, std::__1::char_traits<char> >, boost::spirit::iterator_policies::default_policy<boost::spirit::iterator_policies::ref_counted, boost::spirit::iterator_policies::no_check, boost::spirit::iterator_policies::buffering_input_iterator, boost::spirit::iterator_policies::split_std_deque> >]

To me, this is either bonkers or the example we copied didn't go into enough detail about how to cluebat the compiler.

But, it is not yet obvious that the behavior of g++ <= 4.6 is the correct behavior; it is just the behavior with which we have gotten the tests to pass for release-critical configurations.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, December 15, 2012 4:40:02 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > The other thing that bothers me is that if we generally expect Stan to work in situations where Boost and Eigen
> > generally work, and we find a configuration where that is not the case, we should presume it is a Stan bug, instead of
> > saying we don't care unless it is a Tier I supported configuration.
>
> I hope nobody thought I disagreed with this.  I just wanted
> to establish a policy whereby we could actually release.
>
> I also don't really want to give ourselves a lot more work
> supporting experimental platforms.  If we had more resources,
> it'd totally make sense to look at all the upcoming platforms
> and options.

I don't think any unreleased compiler version should ever be release-critical. But it is good to test Stan with beta versions of compilers and whatnot so that issues can get resolved before the compiler gets released. I know that GCC says that its C++11 support is experimental, although it will be pretty complete for 4.8. But for LLVM, it isn't even experimental. Its website claims that "libc++ is a 100% complete C++11 implementation on Apple's OS X." (I'm not sure that holds for Linux, so my difficulties with it may not be completely representative). As of Monday, clang++ 3.2 will be released as stable. And stanc with O > 0 will fail on every file with that combination, despite having no (known) C++11 specific features.

Ben

Boost uses all sorts of clever typelist reorderings in
order to support using any number of template params in
any order.

> To me, this is either bonkers or the example we copied didn't go into enough detail about how to cluebat the compiler.

Probably both.   I'm regretting in many ways going with the
Spirit Qi parser -- it's been no end of headaches.   It's what
originally crushed and continues to crush the Windows-based
compile/link (blows out memory or segfaults).

It'd be a big deal to swap out at this point, but not impossible.

> But, it is not yet obvious that the behavior of g++ <= 4.6 is the correct behavior; it is just the behavior with which
> we have gotten the tests to pass for release-critical configurations.

I really hope we can figure it out!

It's possible there's a bug in either the g++ <= 4.6 or in
g++ > 4.6.

What I always worry about is the fact that the spec doesn't
nail down some behavior, so that kind of thing can change
in a way that's not technically a bug, but could induce this
kind of problem.

- Bob

I didn't see anywhere in our code where that was happening but I didn't know where to go from there.

Yuanjun,

Great work.

Clock ticks are CPU cycles -- you can convert to time by using the "CLOCKS_PER_SEC" macro.  For example,

clock_t start = clock();
// Do something
clock_t end = clock();

double deltaT = (double)(end - start) / CLOCKS_PER_SEC

I'd actually be interested to see a high dimensional example.  From my experience with RMHMC the pathologies in high-dimensional likelihoods actually scale worse than N^{2}, so the dense mass matrix can still be beneficial.

-Mike

One possibility that occurred to me after sleeping on it
is that some of the subgrammars might not be getting
initialized properly.  This would lead to the same kind of
behavior that Daniel was talking about when things weren't getting
built properly in Windows due to size problems.

Could someone do a sanity check on the way I coded the grammars
I describe below.

(Another check would be to test whether the grammars worked before
I added the subgrammar business for comparison and boolean ops and
if-then and while statements.)

The last thing I had to do to shrink the size of the individual
translation units for statements and expressions was to doubly
link the structures involved in the recursive grammars.

The grammar looks like this from 10,000 feet:

   A1 -> A2 -> ... -> AM -> ... -> AN -> A1

In practice, say A1 is an expression with addition operators,
A2 the rule for multiplicative operators, etc., down to basic
expressions AN, which include parenthesized expressions of
precedence A1.

So I created two grammars, one for A1, and one cut in the middle
for  AM, and had the A1 grammar construct the AM grammar by
passing a self-pointer as a reference.   Here are the relevant
code snippets.

     Techical grammar aside:  the "allow_lte" flag in the ctor
     indicates where to start in the expression tree in order to resolve
     the ambiguity the parser sees in evaluating the final

        int<lower = 0> x;
        int< lower = 0>b > x;

     The second form is illegal and its intent must be expressed as

        real<lower = (0 > b)> x;

expression_grammar.hpp
--------------------------------------------------
...
     template <typename Iterator>
     struct expression_grammar
       : public boost::spirit::qi::grammar<Iterator,
                                           expression(),
                                           whitespace_grammar<Iterator> > {

       expression_grammar(variable_map& var_map,
                          std::stringstream& error_msgs,
                          bool allow_lte = true);

       variable_map& var_map_;
       std::stringstream& error_msgs_;
       term_grammar<Iterator> term_g;
...
-------------------------------------------------------

expression_grammar_def.hpp.
-----------------------------------------------
....
   template <typename Iterator>
     expression_grammar<Iterator>::expression_grammar(variable_map& var_map,
                                                      std::stringstream& error_msgs,
                                                      bool allow_lte)
       : expression_grammar::base_type(allow_lte ? expression_r : expression07_r),
         var_map_(var_map),
         error_msgs_(error_msgs),
         term_g(var_map,error_msgs,*this)
     {
...
---------------------------------------------------

/term_grammar.hpp
----------------------------------------------------
...

     struct term_grammar
       : public boost::spirit::qi::grammar<Iterator,
                                           expression(),

                    std::stringstream& error_msgs,

messages.body_plain:
I should've also said that the other culprit in the parsing is
the iterator.  Those seem to be where some of the other error
messages crept in.  If those aren't returning the expected
characters, you could also see this kind of problem where the
parser's expecting to find a model specification and never finds
it.  (This could be because of pushback errors in buffering or
who knows what in C++11, etc. -- it did look like some of the
basic iterator interfaces changed, which may be why some of the
earlier errors we saw crept in.)

More inline below on specific issues.

On 12/16/12 1:21 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Sunday, December 16, 2012 3:00:13 AM UTC-5, Daniel Lee wrote:

...

> --- Translating Stan graphical model to C++ code ---
> bin/stanc src/test/gm/model_specs/function_signatures7.stan --o=src/test/gm/model_specs/function_signatures7.cpp
> Model name=function_signatures7_model
> Input file=src/test/gm/model_specs/function_signatures7.stan
> Output file=src/test/gm/model_specs/function_signatures7.cpp
>
> INVALID COMMAND-LINE ARGUMENT
> EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=src/test/gm/model_specs/function_signatures7.stan; line=188, column=1
>
>
>   ^-- here
>
>
> DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
> Parser expecting: "*/"
>
> Execute "stanc --help" for more information
> |
>
> Those are weird tokens to be expecting, but at least they do match up with parts of the (grepped) warning novel (look
> for two ### inserted below):

Actually, it's looking for "*/" if it sees an opening
comment.  So the first thing in the file is going to
be a "/*" open comment, and I'm guessing it somehow mangles
the middle and never finds the closing "*/".

>
> |
> goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ grep -A 1 "requested here\|warning: returning" /tmp/clang_warnings.txt
> lib/boost_1.52.0/boost/iterator/iterator_adaptor.hpp:306:18: warning: returning reference to local temporary object
> [-Wreturn-stack-address]
>          { return *m_iterator; }
> --
>        boost::forward_traversal_tag, boost::use_default, boost::use_default>::dereference' requested here
>            return f.dereference();

This is where it's trying to do the buffering -- this is
all encoded in forward-type iterators, which are then wrapped
in buffering iterators.

...

> --
>        boost::spirit::char_encoding::ascii> >, 0> &>, 2> >' requested here
>          = ( omit["/*"] >> *(char_ - "*/") > omit["*/"] ) ###
> --

This rule's ignoring any further "/*" because they don't nest, then
looking for a sequence of chars, stopping before it finds a "*/"
--- that's the   *(char_ - "*/") part.  Then it just jumps over
the last "*/" using "omit".

The point is that there's lots of implicit lookahead every time you consume
a char within a comment to make sure it's not followed by a "*/".

...

> lib/boost_1.52.0/boost/iterator/iterator_adaptor.hpp:306:18: warning: returning reference to local temporary object
> [-Wreturn-stack-address]
>          { return *m_iterator; }

I don't know if this warning is benign or not.  This
is partly why I'm worried about the fact that the
C++11 standard changed the internal type returns inside
the base iterator type we're using:

	std::istreambuf_iterator<char>

Here's the link again, indicating changed behavior as of g++ 4.7:

http://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=50336

http://gcc.1065356.n5.nabble.com/Bug-libstdc-50336-New-LWG-issue-445-td347525.html

>        > >::************>::failed' requested here
>        BOOST_CONCEPT_USAGE(InputIterator)

This is a new thing in Boost 1.52 that checks if a type
implements the appropriate set of concepts to be used
to instantiate a type.  I believe if it doesn't, Boost
relies on the substitution failure is not an error (SFINAE)
pattern, which is why you'd see something like the above.

So anotehr possibility would be to back off to Boost 1.51
and see if that's working with the parser.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Those autocorrelation plots in figure 2 look awesome.
This is fantastic progress -- can't wait to see what
you come up with when you're not working on finals!

If I understand what you have now in table 1, it's just
overall time for 10^5 samples and expected leapfrog
steps per sample.

I'm thinking the results are even better than your report.

What we really care about is time to useful number of
effective samples (say 100 per parameter).  That means
running multiple chains (let's say 4) and making sure
all parameters pass the R-hat diagnostic test (R-hat < 1.1).

I suggest measuring the following for convergence time

   1.  # of iterations to converge (4 chains, all params Rhat < 1.1)
   2.  avg # leapfrog steps / iteration
   3.  cost / leapfrog step
   4.  => time to converge

and the following for mixing after convergence

   1.  # of iterations / effective sample
   2.  avg time / iteration
   3.  => time / effective sample at convergence

The more I think about things like the way our tests behave,
the more I think we need to run these multiple times with
different inits and look at variance.  I wouldn't be at all
surprised if the full mass matrix turns out to be more robust
than a diagonal mass in some cases and less so in others.

The leapfrog calcs, and in particular the gradients,
do indeed dwarf the rest of the calcs being done in NUTS.

Next, I'd try to test the effect of dimensionality that
you discuss at the end of the pdf.  This might also get
at the robustness.

There are really three ways to scale that we care about:

1.  more data (does not increase dimensionality, does increase leapfrog time)

2.  more parameters

3.  more complex models (e.g., hierarchical or time series)

- Bob

I'll definitely perform multiple chain analysis for a higher dimensional example which is less trivial.

You can do

for i in {1..4}
do
  ./model --refresh=0 --seed=12345 --chain_id=$i --samples=samples$i.csv &
done

which will background each process and essentially do four chains in parallel (assuming you have at least four cores to work with). RStan v1.0.4 has functions to read the four samples*.csv files into a stanfit object, which can calculate Rhats, n_effs, etc.

Ben

> Those autocorrelation plots in figure 2 look awesome.
> This is fantastic progress -- can't wait to see what

> If I understand what you have now in table 1, it's just
> overall time for 10^5 samples and expected leapfrog
> steps per sample.
>
> I'm thinking the results are even better than your report.
>
> What we really care about is time to useful number of
> effective samples (say 100 per parameter).  That means
> running multiple chains (let's say 4) and making sure
> all parameters pass the R-hat diagnostic test (R-hat < 1.1).
>
> I suggest measuring the following for convergence time
>
>  1.  # of iterations to converge (4 chains, all params Rhat < 1.1)
>  2.  avg # leapfrog steps / iteration
>  3.  cost / leapfrog step
>  4.  => time to converge
>
> and the following for mixing after convergence
>
>  1.  # of iterations / effective sample
>  2.  avg time / iteration
>  3.  => time / effective sample at convergence
>
> The more I think about things like the way our tests behave,
> the more I think we need to run these multiple times with
> different inits and look at variance.  I wouldn't be at all
> surprised if the full mass matrix turns out to be more robust
> than a diagonal mass in some cases and less so in others.
>
> The leapfrog calcs, and in particular the gradients,
> do indeed dwarf the rest of the calcs being done in NUTS.
>
> Next, I'd try to test the effect of dimensionality that
> you discuss at the end of the pdf.  This might also get
> at the robustness.
>
> There are really three ways to scale that we care about:
>
> 1.  more data (does not increase dimensionality, does increase leapfrog time)
>
> 2.  more parameters
>
> 3.  more complex models (e.g., hierarchical or time series)
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif
messages.body_plain:
Cool!

While we're talking about Hessians and autodiff, I think it'd be
awesome if someday we had the ability to autodiff ourselves just the
diagonal of the Hessian in linear time. That would open the door to an
efficient implementation of a general-purpose variational inference
algorithm in Stan.

Matt

On Thu, Dec 13, 2012 at 11:10 AM, Michael Betancourt
<betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Uncle Bob!  Awesome.
>
> On Dec 13, 2012, at 1:15 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>> To lead with the punchline, we can pretty easily and
>> efficiently implement arbitrary Hessian-vector (or
>> row vector-Hessian) products in a single pass of efficient
>> forward auto-dif followed by reverse mode auto-dif of
>> the result.
>>
>> Michael and I spent part of his first day talking
>> about how we could do Hessian-vector products with auto-diff.
>> He gave me enough hints on the so-called R operator that I could
>> work out the algebra and auto-dif implementation from scratch.
>>
>> This will be useful for RM-HMC and for optimizations
>> using curvature info.
>>
>> On 12/12/12 4:09 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>>
>> > Efficient Hessian-Vector Products:
>> >
>> > Bishop 5.4.6
>> > http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.29.6143
>> > http://justindomke.wordpress.com/2009/01/17/hessian-vector-products/
>>
>> What helped me the most was the doc for Theano:
>>
>>  http://deeplearning.net/software/theano/tutorial/gradients.html
>>
>> which presented it in a more computer-sciency way than most of
>> the other applied math and physics thing I looked at (like Bishop).
>>
>> I then worked through the algebra and derived the R operator myself,
>> which is pretty trivial.  As an upside, I can now follow the discussion
>> in Bishop, which I never understood before.
>>
>> The key is noticing that if H is the Hessian of y w.r.t. x and v
>> is any old vector, then the first step is noting that:
>>
>>   H * v = grad_x ((grad_x y)' * v)
>>
>> Then we use a little of the old lambda abstraction to create an
>> operator:
>>
>>  R = lambda y. [ v' * (grad_x y) ]
>>
>> so that
>>
>>  R(y) =  v' * grad_x y
>>
>>       =  v1 * dy/dx1 + v2 * dy/dx2 + ... + vK * dy/dxK
>>
>> and
>>
>>  H * v = grad_x R(y)
>>
>> The key to making it efficient in auto-dif is to compute R(y) using
>> a forward-mode auto dif, then do the outer grad_x using reverse mode
>> on the result.  And the beauty is we only need to implement standard
>> templated forward-mode auto-dif once in a simple templated way and
>> we can then use it to do these calculations with the right initializations ---
>> the adjoint of x_k is initialized to v_k and Bob's your uncle.
>>
>> The whole calc will probably take on the order of 2 or 3 times the
>> time for the basic gradient, so about 10 times the cost of the function
>> eval itself.
>>
>> I've already implemented most of the basic forward dif, though I pulled
>> it out of version control ages ago because we weren't using it for anything.
>>
>> After the next release, I'll pull it back into the main branch and then we
>> only have to implement gradients for special functions (which is much much
>> eaiser to do efficiently than reverse mode).
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>> --
>>
>>
>

> --
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif
messages.body_plain:
It's not totally straightforward to do it in linear time. Not insanely
complicated, but not as straightforward as Hessian-vector products.

Basically, I think it winds up looking a lot like reverse-mode AD, but
instead of leveraging
∂/∂x_i f(g(x)) = ∂f/∂g ∂g/∂x_i,
which only involves first derivatives, you have to use
∂^2/∂x_i^2 f(g(x)) = ∂^2 f/∂g^2 (∂g/∂x_i)^2 + ∂f/∂g ∂^2 g/∂x_i^2
which involves a bunch of second derivatives. Those might be
implementable using the Hessian-vector product trick, though.

It'd probably be a reasonable amount of work to implement this, so it
may not be a first-tier priority, but it'd be great to have someday. I
don't think any other autodiff package has the ability to compute
diagonal Hessians in linear time, and it's a useful thing to have
sometimes.

Matt

messages.subject: auto-dif refs
messages.body_plain:
The cleanest refs I've found for auto-dif are the following.
This one's clearly the basis for the discussion on Wikipedia, but
there's more on the handout:

   http://www.pvv.ntnu.no/~berland/resources/autodiff-triallecture.pdf

This one's particularly nice in terms of notational development
and application to matrix ops:

   http://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/gilesm/files/AD2008.pdf

This is where we need to go next for efficiency of multivariate
models -- that is, do all the solvers, etc., on double matrices.
Shouldn't be too hard given that there are decent ways to do

   B / A = B * A^{-1}

and

   A \ B = A^{-1} * B

so we can still avoid inverses even in the auto-dif calcs.

- Bob
