messages.subject: Stan 1.1.0 and RStan 1.1.0
messages.body_plain:
We're happy to announce the availability of Stan and RStan
versions 1.1.0.  Information on downloading and installing and
using them is available as always from the Stan home page:

    http://mc-stan.org/

v1.1.0 Release Notes
======================================================================
-- Backward Compatibility Issue
    * Categorical distribution recoded to match documentation;  it
      now has support {1,...,K} rather than {0,...,K-1}.
    * (RStan) change default value of permuted flag from FALSE to TRUE for
      Stan fit S4 extract() method
-- New Features
    * Conditional (if-then-else) statements
    * While statements
-- New Functions
    * generalized multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose() to non-square
      matrices
    * special functions: log_inv_logit(), log1m_inv_logit()
    * matrix special functions: cumulative_sum()
    * probability functions: poisson_log_log() for log-rate
      parameterized Poisson
    * matrix functions: block(), diag_pre_multiply(), diag_post_multiply()
    * comparison operators (<, >, <=, >=, ==, !=)
    * boolean operators (!, ||, &&)
    * allow +/- inf values in variable declaration constraints
-- RStan Improvements
    * get_posterior_mean() method for Stan fit objects
    * replaced RcppEigen dependency with include of Eigen source
    * added read_stan_csv() to create Stan fit object from CSV files of
      the form written to disk by the command-line version of Stan
    * as.data.frame() S3 method for Stan fit objects
-- Bug Fixes
    * fixed bug in NUTS diagonal resulting in too small step sizes
    * fixed bug introduced in 1.0.3 that hid line and column number
      bug reporting
    * added checks that data dimensions match as well as sizes
    * removed non-symmetric versions of eigenvalues() and eigenvectors()
    * testing identifiers are not reserved words in C++/Stan
    * trapping/reporting locations of errors in data and init reads
    * improvements in dump data format reader for more R compatibility
      and more generality
    * fix bug in bernoulli logit distro tail density
-- Code Improvements
    * templated out matrix libs to reduce code duplication
    * vectorized auto-dif for tcrossprod() and crossprod()
    * optimizations in Wishart
    * vectorization with efficiency improvements in probability distributions
-- Libraries Updated
    * Eigen version 3.1.1 replaced with version 3.1.2
    * Boost version 1.51.0 replaced with version 1.52.0
-- Manual Improvements
    * New chapter on univariate and multivariate variable transforms
    * Many consistency improvements and typo corrections
    * Information on running command line in parallel from shell

====================================================================

Enjoy, and let us know if you run into any problems.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] sorted out Hessian-vector products for auto-dif
messages.body_plain:
To clarify, when I said "a reasonable amount of work" I meant "a lot of work."

I wonder if an alternative could be found to coding all of the
2nd-order derivatives. We only need them so that we can multiply them
by gradients, which means we don't need to form them explicitly at
all. Maybe there's a way to implement it that only touches the base
vari class.

The connection to variational inference is in my ICML paper with Sam
Gershman, which uses Taylor approximations to do VB, approximating the
posterior with a mixture of isotropic Gaussians:
http://icml.cc/discuss/2012/360.html
The only obstacle to implementing it in Stan is the lack of cheap
diagonal Hessians. I may implement it in Stan soon with the N^2
diagonal Hessian calculation anyway, actually.

Matt

>> instead of leveraging
>> ∂/∂x_i f(g(x)) = ∂f/∂g ∂g/∂x_i,
>> which only involves first derivatives, you have to use

>> which involves a bunch of second derivatives. Those might be
>> implementable using the Hessian-vector product trick, though.
>
>

> would be linear.

>

> infrastructe wouldn't be hard (that is, the equivalent to var and
> vari, say var2nd and vari2nd).
>
> - Bob

On 12/17/12 6:21 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> To clarify, when I said "a reasonable amount of work" I meant "a lot of work."

I think very different about two kinds of work.  The first
is hard work like building a brick wall -- it doesn't need
any technology innovation, but there's lots of hard work.
That's what second-order auto-dif's like.

The other kind of hard work is like that involved in NUTS.
Lots of brain work required first, but then when it's sorted,
not much coding effort.

> I wonder if an alternative could be found to coding all of the
> 2nd-order derivatives. We only need them so that we can multiply them
> by gradients, which means we don't need to form them explicitly at
> all. Maybe there's a way to implement it that only touches the base
> vari class.

So you only need a (diagonal Hessian)-gradient product?
That should be much easier.

Michael B just laid a tensor (third-order derivative) matrix
trace problem on me today, which I think can also be simplified
with auto-dif.

Writing this stuff out in text or on paper is harder than coding
the basic systems.  The Hessian calc's only six or seven lines of
code on top of fwd and reverse auto-dif!

> The connection to variational inference is in my ICML paper with Sam
> Gershman, which uses Taylor approximations to do VB, approximating the
> posterior with a mixture of isotropic Gaussians:
> http://icml.cc/discuss/2012/360.html
> The only obstacle to implementing it in Stan is the lack of cheap
> diagonal Hessians. I may implement it in Stan soon with the N^2
> diagonal Hessian calculation anyway, actually.

Cool.  We should prioritize getting all the forward-mode auto-difs
done, then.  It'll still be 3n or so worse than computing just
the probability function, though.

- Bob

messages.subject: Speed Results
messages.body_plain:
I created a wiki page to compare speed the speed models across configurations:

https://code.google.com/p/stan/wiki/SpeedResults

Unlike the test-unit results where we are fishing for bugs, here I think we only need to compare the best versions of each compiler for whatever the optimal level of optimization is (I've done O3 for now, but for me O2 is about the same for execution and somewhat faster for compilation). It would be good if someone could put some Mac results up there. Windows, too, I guess although any compiler other than the one included in Rtools is probably a headache to get working.

Note that the wiki is a separate git repo

https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/checkout?repo=wiki

And rather than using the web interface, it is probably easier to clone, edit that page with a text editor, add, commit, and push.

Ben

P.S. We have got to do something about the schools model in vol2.

On Thursday, December 20, 2012 2:18:35 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > On Dec 19, 2012, at 4:33 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> I'm sort of amazed at the variation in compilers
> across models.  But then maybe that's random init
> differences?  Are they all running with the same seed?

Same seed. TFC includes scarcely more than this R function

bench <- function(i) {
  mark <- "elapsed"
  compile <- system.time(fit <- stan_demo(i, chains = 0, iter = 0))[mark]
  execute <- system.time(fit <- stan_demo(i, fit = fit, seed = 12345, refresh = -1))[mark]
  if (length(dim(fit)) == 0) execute <- NA_real_ # failure
  return(c(compile, execute))
}

which is executed on each .stan file. Something could be said for increasing the number of observations so that we have fewer examples that take a tenth of a second to execute, but that would be killer for the examples that take minutes to execute.

> And it's time to generalize the Matt trick to multivariate
> models for alpha in vol2/schools/schools.stan

We do have stuff in the manual about that. More generally, are the bugs_examples intended to be literal translations of BUGS examples or should we be tricking them out? In a couple of cases, we have both an unvectorized and a vectorized version of the model, but that is not so helpful when the unvectorized version is unreasonably slow.

Ben

The issue is that one of our distributions is improperly formatting the error message. That throws a different type of exception. My guess is that we don't catch that particular exception in the leapfrog step and it dies.

My guess is that it's happening in either the multi_normal or inv_wishart distributions. I'm pretty sure the univariate tests would catch this error.

I'll try to hunt it down and fix it.

Daniel

messages.subject: BUGS/JAGS models: clarity vs. speed
messages.body_plain:
On 12/20/12 2:59 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, December 20, 2012 2:18:35 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:

>     And it's time to generalize the Matt trick to multivariate
>     models for alpha in vol2/schools/schools.stan
>
>
> We do have stuff in the manual about that. More generally, are the bugs_examples intended to be literal translations of
> BUGS examples or should we be tricking them out?

The BUGS examples are being used for both evaluation
and pedagogy.

For both purposes, we want to leave the models themselves
unchanged (I'd be OK with reparameterizations where convenient)

The JAGS versions modify the BUGS versions in
some cases.  We decided ages ago to take the JAGS versions
as our basis.

For evaluation, it's clear we should do efficient
implementations.

On the pedagogy side,  we have the conflicting goals
of clarity and speed.

> In a couple of cases, we have both an unvectorized and a vectorized
> version of the model, but that is not so helpful when the unvectorized version is unreasonably slow.

I see room for two versions -- one clear and one fast.

I share your notion of clarity.

The Matt trick's clarity is probably an issue with
habit.  In some ways, it's clearer to think of
a bunch of normal variates getting rescaled than to
think about drawing from all sorts of differently scaled
and located distributions.

I think having to create a vector and write into it
for vectorization is less clear for everyone.

The main reason plain old vectorization may be less
clear is that it's not immediately evident to either
the BUGS or R user how we've vectorized.  That is,
we allow any of the arguments to be a scalar that's
just repeated.  Most R functions won't let you do that,
will they?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 12/22/12 3:24 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> The compiler errors I have hit with double_exponential under llvm-g++ are not our fault, since I can reproduce the
> problem just by trying to compile
>
> |
> goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp$ cat sign.cpp
> #include <boost/math/special_functions/sign.hpp>
> #include <iostream>
> int main() {
>    std::cout << "expect 1, get " << boost::math::sign(10.0) << std::endl;
>    std::cout << "expect 0, get " << boost::math::sign(0.0) << std::endl;
>    std::cout << "expect -1, get " << boost::math::sign(-5.0) << std::endl;
>    return 0;
> }
> |
>
> but we can work around it by defining our own sign() function instead of using boost's, e.g. this patch
>
> |
> diff --git a/src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/double_exponential.hpp
> b/src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/double_exponential.hpp
> index ccea83a..f2c14d2 100644
> --- a/src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/double_exponential.hpp
> +++ b/src/stan/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/double_exponential.hpp
> @@ -7,11 +7,15 @@
>   #include <stan/meta/traits.hpp>
>   #include <stan/prob/constants.hpp>
>   #include <stan/prob/traits.hpp>
> -#include <boost/math/special_functions/sign.hpp>
> +//#include <boost/math/special_functions/sign.hpp>
>
>   namespace stan {
>
>     namespace prob {
> +    template<typename T>
> +    inline int sign(T& z) {
> +      return (z == 0) ? 0 : z < 0 ? -1 : 1;
> +    }
>
>       // DoubleExponential(y|mu,sigma)  [sigma > 0]
>       // FIXME: add documentation
> @@ -32,7 +36,7 @@ namespace stan {
>         using stan::prob::include_summand;
>         using std::log;
>         using std::fabs;
> -      using boost::math::sign;
> + //     using boost::math::sign;
> |
>
> I have not figured out why boost's implementation of the sign function
>
> http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_52_0/boost/math/special_functions/sign.hpp
>
> is so complicated.

It's Boost --- I think they award a prize to the most obfuscated
API each year.

And the complex part isn't even in the above linked file, it's in
the traits class that's included.

 > I'm sure there is a reason,

All they're doing is using some trait template metaprogramming
to sort out the floating point representation so that they can mask
out the sign bit rather than doing a comparison operation.  And do
efficient sign changes on platforms that support it.

 > but I doubt that reason is relevant to Stan.

I wish we had efficiency concerns at that level.  But as of now,
we should just go with Ben's more straightforward comparison-based code.

(I don't know what the boundary conditions of sign() are supposed to be for
NaN given that the return is an int, but I don't think it matters
for us one way or another.)

> With that patch I can get llvm-g++ to pass test-unit and so far it has not broken any other configuration I have tried.
> I doubt many people would really want to use llvm-g++, but it does get us closer to being able to do on Linux what Xcode
> does on the Mac, except Xcode is using 4.2.1 and I am using 4.6. Does anyone see a compelling reason to stick with
> boost's sign function?

Not at all.  Could you just merge that patch into master?

- Bob

Honestly, I'm confused by it too. The documentation is here:

On 12/23/12 1:13 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> I pushed a bunch of univariate cumulatives and value tests -- only negative binomial and beta-binomial are missing.  One word of caution -- don't trust the binomial or Bernoulli CDFs at the moment as there are likely some compliment issues and off-by-one argument issues I need to sit down and figure out without a sinus headache.

Awesome -- if you send me the LaTeX for the PDF
you sent me before, I can drop it into the manual.

If you'd rather do it yourself, the relevant doc's in

    /src/docs/stan-reference/functions.tex

The \fitem{} function defined in stan-manuals.sty formats and
enters a label for the index.  I'll probably also be modifying
that file because I'm going to add the binomial_logit parameterization
(and vectorize the gradients in binomial while I'm at it) -- got
sidetracked after looking at the very first BUGS model!

For the manual, is it OK with everyone if we use F(x) for cumulative
distribution functions rather than the P(x) Michael used?  I think
we want to say something like:

    The cumulative distribution function F(x) for the distribution
    Normal(mu,sigma) is

       F(x) = Phi((x - mu)/sigma).

Or even F(y) if Andrew feels strongly about his x is for predictors,
y is for variables thing?  On p. 25 of BDA, Andrew defines the cumulative
as

    F(v_*) = Pr(v <= v_*)

where v is a random variable and v_* a bound variable.

The notational issue is that lower case letters (like v) are overloaded
as random or bound variables in BDA's notation, leading to awkwardness
in translating the usual idiom

    If X is a random variable such that X ~ Normal(mu,sigma), then

      F_X(x) = Pr(X < x) = Phi((x - mu)/sigma).

I like the BDA notation for applied modeling, as in the Stan modeling language!
It's really clumsy to try to try to capitalize Greek letters, vectors,
matrices, etc.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Bob
I think n_eff=1 might be some sort of minimum.  If you'd prefer, we can have it return n_eff=.1.  Currently it's returning n_eff=10 which isn't right at all.  In general I don't want to be returning NA's or Nan's.  These are not really NA's or Nan's; we just have a particular formula for R.hat and n.eff that we haven't adapted to work with chains of length 5.  That's fine--I don't think we need to kill ourselves coming up with a definition that works with chains of length 5, but when it doesn't work, I'd rather have it report a number that clearly represents DOES_NOT_CONVERGE (e.g., Rhat=5 and n_eff=1 (or, if you'd prefer, n_eff=0.1).  I guess what I'm saying is, this is not a 0/0 situation.  It's just a situation where we have not gone to the trouble of being super-cereful in the definition of R.hat, and I think it makes more sense to kluge it by giving R.hat a large value, than to kluge it by returning NA or Nan.

Where are you including them from?

We're using the lgamma() and digamma() implementations from
Boost.  These should work the same way on every platform.
To make sure you get those, call:

    boost::math::lgamma()

and

   boost::math::digamma()

 > But on Mac, gamma is really the gamma in math.  So
> I guess we should never use "gamma" literally in C/C++.

I'm not quite sure what you mean by "literally".

In some cases, we have things like this in a block:

   template <typename T>
   ...
   {
     using boost::math::lgamma;

     T x;

     T y = lgamma(x);

   }

What happens here is that you get the lgamma from Boost
unless T is stan::agrad::var, in which case argument-dependent
lookup gives you the lgamma function defined in stan::agrad.

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument-dependent_name_lookup

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I understand that it's OK to have a piecewise
estimator that does different things for different
sample size.

I'm just saying I'm uncomfortable over-estimating something
like effective sample size.  Could we just make R-hat
equal to infinity and n_eff = 0?  Those are at least
not NaN values.

I still don't understand what post-processing you need
an R-hat value for and n_eff value for if we don't have
any effective samples yet.

- Bob

On 12/26/12 9:48 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Bob
> I think n_eff=1 might be some sort of minimum.  If you'd prefer, we can have it return n_eff=.1.  Currently it's returning n_eff=10 which isn't right at all.  In general I don't want to be returning NA's or Nan's.  These are not really NA's or Nan's; we just have a particular formula for R.hat and n.eff that we haven't adapted to work with chains of length 5.  That's fine--I don't think we need to kill ourselves coming up with a definition that works with chains of length 5, but when it doesn't work, I'd rather have it report a number that clearly represents DOES_NOT_CONVERGE (e.g., Rhat=5 and n_eff=1 (or, if you'd prefer, n_eff=0.1).  I guess what I'm saying is, this is not a 0/0 situation.  It's just a situation where we have not gone to the trouble of being super-cereful in the definition of R.hat, and I think it makes more sense to kluge it by giving R.hat a large value, than to kluge it by returning NA or Nan.
> A
>
> On Dec 26, 2012, at 9:38 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>>
>> On 12/26/12 4:52 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>>> We could change to NA or even have it default (when it's NA or Inf or Nan) to the number of iterations per chain (5, in
>>> this case).  Or we could have n_eff default to 1.  I don't think we want NA's etc because that gets in the way with
>>> post-processeing.
>>
>> I'd prefer NaN returns.  What post-processing does it screw up?
>> If it's just visualization in plot(), maybe we should change plot().
>>
>> What I don't want to do is tell people we have 1 effective sample
>> (or even worse, tell them we have 5 effective samples), when we
>> probably don't have any.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>> --
>>
>

On Thu, Dec 27, 2012 at 3:53 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> n 12/27/12 12:27 AM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> > By the way, I have the experience that using gamma intended to be the gamma function in math in C on Linux, on which
> > gamma is actually log gamma and tgamma (true gamma) should be used.
>
> Where are you including them from?
>
> We're using the lgamma() and digamma() implementations from
> Boost.  These should work the same way on every platform.
> To make sure you get those, call:
>
>    boost::math::lgamma()
>
> and
>
>   boost::math::digamma()
>
>
> > But on Mac, gamma is really the gamma in math.  So
> > I guess we should never use "gamma" literally in C/C++.
>
> I'm not quite sure what you mean by "literally".
>
> In some cases, we have things like this in a block:
>
>   template <typename T>
>   ...
>   {
>     using boost::math::lgamma;
>
>     T x;
>
>     T y = lgamma(x);
>
>   }
>
> What happens here is that you get the lgamma from Boost
> unless T is stan::agrad::var, in which case argument-dependent
> lookup gives you the lgamma function defined in stan::agrad.
>
>   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argument-dependent_name_lookup

>
>
> - Bob
>
> --
>
>

messages.subject: Rtools only 32 bit?
messages.body_plain:
g++ itself is a 32-bit program from Rtools?  Can it
still compile 64-bit executables for 64-bit R?

The 32-bit limitation is really too bad because of the
amount of memory we want in the compiler.  This could
be very limiting for Windows users.

Is there somewhere we can point people to get instructions
on swappin gin a 64-bit compiler?

- Bob

On 12/28/12 9:51 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> Just to point out that the gcc in Rtools is 32 bits program, which cannot take advantage of all the RAM in a 64 bits OS.

from http://sourceforge.net/projects/mingw-w64/files/Toolchains%20targetting%20Win64/Personal%20Builds/rubenvb/gcc-4.7-release/ and a lot of other places.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] compiler warnings
messages.body_plain:
Thanks.  I'll try to knock out everything but the long
long issues -- those are from 64-bit Windows defining
size_t equal to unsigned long long (unliked unsigned long
everywhere else).  So I think it'll take some typedefs
to do this right or the introduction of Boost's fixed
size types (which we maybe should've been doing all along).

The variable length arrays are inside sizeof() calcs, so
that's just some arithmetic.  Most of the rest looks like
extra variables and functions and missing punctuation or
spaces.

- Bob

messages.subject: fixed most of the warnings
messages.body_plain:
I fixed most of the warnings.  Almost all of them were
false positives, at least in terms of things we care about,
but I fixed many that I could anyway.

I've grouped the ones that are left (see below).  There
are cases I think the code's OK as is, the long long case
we need to fix with some ifdefs or explicitly sized int defs,
and some issues in the test framework I'm going to leave to
Daniel.  I think we can fix the unused vars in generated
code, too.

Some ones I couldn't fix involve false positive reports on
unused variables -- you need them there because they supply
default values.

The library code in Boost and Eigen spews an enormous number
of warnings now that we have the warning level turned up.
Most for the same silly reasons as our code had so many warnings.

Most of the warning were from unused variables in parameters
lists (I just wrapped in /* */).  Also a bunch of files
without terminating newlines.

The only things that even looked like they could be issues
actually wouldn't be given the way the test code would've
executed (I fixed anyway by initialization variables).

- Bob
